nodes.title: Approximating discrete probability distributions with dependence trees
nodes.access_note: Paywalled (IEEE). Abstract and bibliographic metadata only.
nodes.abstract: A method is presented to approximate optimally an n-dimensional discrete probability distribution by a product of second-order distributions, or the distribution of the first-order tree dependence. The problem is to find an optimum set of n - 1 first order dependence relationship among the n variables. It is shown that the procedure derived in this paper yields an approximation of a minimum difference in information. It is further shown that when this procedure is applied to empirical observations from an unknown distribution of tree dependence, the procedure is the maximum-likelihood estimate of the distribution.
nodes.key_problem: Approximate an n-dimensional discrete probability distribution by a product of second-order (pairwise) distributions arranged as a tree of dependencies.
methods: Choose the optimal set of n-1 first-order dependence relationships (the optimal dependence tree)
Maximum-likelihood estimation of a tree-dependent distribution from empirical observations
findings: The procedure yields the approximation with minimum difference in information
Applied to samples from a tree-dependent distribution, it is the maximum-likelihood estimate
limitations: All variables are assumed to be observed - no hidden (latent) variables (cf. Choi et al. 2011, p.3: 'the Chow-Liu tree for the observed variables without any hidden nodes')
Restricted to tree-structured dependence
Organiser read abstract only
evidence_refs: Choi et al. 2011 Sec. 5.1 reviews the algorithm (p.14)

nodes.title: Multicast topology inference from measured end-to-end loss
nodes.access_note: Paywalled (IEEE). Abstract and bibliographic metadata only.
nodes.abstract: The use of multicast inference on end-to-end measurement has recently been proposed as a means to infer network internal characteristics such as packet link loss rate and delay. In this paper, we propose three types of algorithm that use loss measurements to infer the underlying multicast topology: i) a grouping estimator that exploits the monotonicity of loss rates with increasing path length; ii) a maximum-likelihood (ML) estimator (MLE); and iii) a Bayesian estimator. We establish their consistency, compare their complexity and accuracy, and analyze the modes of failure and their asymptotic probabilities.
nodes.key_problem: Infer the logical topology of a multicast tree from loss measurements made only at the receivers.
methods: Grouping estimator exploiting monotonicity of loss rates with increasing path length
Maximum-likelihood topology estimator
Bayesian topology estimator
findings: Consistency of the three estimators is established
Complexity, accuracy and asymptotic failure probabilities are compared
limitations: Requires multicast probing support
Organiser read abstract only; algorithmic details need full-text review

nodes.title: The neighbor-joining method: a new method for reconstructing phylogenetic trees
nodes.access_note: Free to read at the publisher (OpenAlex oa_status: bronze). Not redistributed; link only.
nodes.abstract: A new method called the neighbor-joining method is proposed for reconstructing phylogenetic trees from evolutionary distance data. The principle of this method is to find pairs of operational taxonomic units (OTUs [= neighbors]) that minimize the total branch length at each stage of clustering of OTUs starting with a starlike tree. The branch lengths as well as the topology of a parsimonious tree can quickly be obtained by using this method. Using computer simulation, we studied the efficiency of this method in obtaining the correct unrooted tree in comparison with that of five other tree-making methods: the unweighted pair group method of analysis, Farris's method, Sattath and Tversky's method, Li's method, and Tateno et al.'s modified Farris method. The new, neighbor-joining method and Sattath and Tversky's method are shown to be generally better than the other methods.
nodes.key_problem: Reconstruct a phylogenetic (evolutionary) tree - topology and branch lengths - from evolutionary distance data between observed taxa.
methods: Neighbor-joining: starting from a star-like tree, repeatedly join the pair of operational taxonomic units (neighbours) that minimises total branch length
Computer simulation comparing tree-building methods
findings: Branch lengths and topology of a parsimonious tree are obtained quickly
Neighbor-joining and Sattath-Tversky's method are generally better than UPGMA, Farris's, Li's and Tateno et al.'s methods in simulation
limitations: Input is a distance matrix: accuracy depends on how well distances are estimated
Evaluation in the abstract is simulation-based
Produces an unrooted tree
Organiser read abstract only

nodes.title: Robust uncertainty principles: exact signal reconstruction from highly incomplete frequency information
nodes.abstract: This paper considers the model problem of reconstructing an object from incomplete frequency samples. Consider a discrete-time signal f∈C^N and a randomly chosen set of frequencies Ω. Is it possible to reconstruct f from the partial knowledge of its Fourier coefficients on the set Ω? A typical result of this paper is as follows. Suppose that f is a superposition of |T| spikes f(t)=Σ_τ∈Tf(τ)δ(t-τ) obeying |T|≤C_M·(log N)^-1 · |Ω| for some constant C_M>0. We do not know the locations of the spikes nor their amplitudes. Then with probability at least 1-O(N^-M), f can be reconstructed exactly as the solution to the ℓ_1 minimization problem. In short, exact recovery may be obtained by solving a convex optimization problem. We give numerical values for C_M which depend on the desired probability of success. Our result may be interpreted as a novel kind of nonlinear sampling theorem. In effect, it says that any signal made out of |T| spikes may be recovered by convex programming from almost every set of frequencies of size O(|T|·logN). Moreover, this is nearly optimal in the sense that any method succeeding with probability 1-O(N^-M) would in general require a number of frequency samples at least proportional to |T|·logN. The methodology extends to a variety of other situations and higher dimensions. For example, we show how one can reconstruct a piecewise constant (one- or two-dimensional) object from incomplete frequency samples - provided that the number of jumps (discontinuities) obeys the condition above - by minimizing other convex functionals such as the total variation of f.
nodes.key_problem: Reconstruct a discrete-time signal from a random, incomplete subset of its Fourier coefficients.
methods: l1-minimisation (convex programming) for sparse 'spike' signals
Total-variation minimisation for piecewise-constant objects
findings: Signals made of |T| spikes are recovered exactly with high probability from O(|T| log N) frequency samples
The sample count is nearly optimal
limitations: Requires the signal to be sparse (or have sparse gradient)
Frequencies chosen at random
The unknown is a signal/image on a known grid - there is no unknown graph or tree topology

nodes.title: Inference of multicast routing trees and bottleneck bandwidths using end-to-end measurements
nodes.access_note: Paywalled (IEEE INFOCOM). Abstract and bibliographic metadata only.
nodes.abstract: The efficacy of end-to-end multicast transport protocols depends critically upon their ability to scale efficiently to a large number of receivers. Several research multicast protocols attempt to achieve this high scalability by identifying sets of co-located receivers in order to enhance loss recovery, congestion control and so forth. A number of these schemes could be enhanced and simplified by some level of explicit knowledge of the topology of the multicast distribution tree, the value of the bottleneck bandwidth along the path between the source and each individual receiver and the approximate location of the bottlenecks in the tree. In this paper, we explore the problem of inferring the internal structure of a multicast distribution tree using only observations made at the end hosts. By noting correlations of loss patterns across the receiver set and by measuring how the network perturbs the fine-grained timing structure of the packets sent from the source, we can determine both the underlying multicast tree structure as well as the bottleneck bandwidths. The simulations show that the algorithm is robust and appears to converge to the correct tree with high probability.
nodes.key_problem: Infer the internal structure of a multicast distribution tree, and the bottleneck bandwidths on it, using only observations made at the end hosts (receivers).
methods: Correlate packet-loss patterns across the receiver set to determine shared tree structure
Measure how the network perturbs fine-grained packet timing to estimate bottleneck bandwidths
findings: In simulation the algorithm is robust and converges to the correct tree with high probability
limitations: Simulation-only evaluation reported in the abstract
Requires IP multicast
Organiser read abstract only - the exact grouping procedure needs full-text review

nodes.title: Learning Latent Tree Graphical Models
nodes.access_note: Open access (arXiv 1009.2722; JMLR). Full text reviewed by organiser.
nodes.abstract: We study the problem of learning a latent tree graphical model where samples are available only from a subset of variables. We propose two consistent and computationally efficient algorithms for learning minimal latent trees, that is, trees without any redundant hidden nodes. Unlike many existing methods, the observed nodes (or variables) are not constrained to be leaf nodes. Our first algorithm, recursive grouping, builds the latent tree recursively by identifying sibling groups using so-called information distances. One of the main contributions of this work is our second algorithm, which we refer to as CLGrouping. CLGrouping starts with a pre-processing procedure in which a tree over the observed variables is constructed. This global step groups the observed nodes that are likely to be close to each other in the true latent tree, thereby guiding subsequent recursive grouping (or equivalent procedures) on much smaller subsets of variables. This results in more accurate and efficient learning of latent trees. We also present regularized versions of our algorithms that learn latent tree approximations of arbitrary distributions. We compare the proposed algorithms to other methods by performing extensive numerical experiments on various latent tree graphical models such as hidden Markov models and star graphs. In addition, we demonstrate the applicability of our methods on real-world datasets by modeling the dependency structure of monthly stock returns in the S&P index and of the words in the 20 newsgroups dataset.
nodes.key_problem: Learn a latent tree graphical model when samples are available only from a subset of the variables (the others are hidden).
methods: Recursive grouping using information distances
CLGrouping: build a Chow-Liu tree over observed variables, then apply recursive grouping or neighbor-joining locally (CLRG / CLNJ)
Regularised versions for approximating arbitrary distributions
findings: The algorithms are consistent with good sample and computational complexity
CLNJ/CLRG outperform NJ and RG on latent trees with large diameter
Applied to S&P 500 monthly returns and the 20 Newsgroups dataset
limitations: Assumes the true structure is a (minimal) latent tree
Analysis focuses on Gaussian and symmetric discrete distributions (Sec. 5)
evidence_refs: Full text arXiv:1009.2722 pp.3-5 (related work), p.10 (Prop. 3), p.14 (Sec. 5), p.25 (experiments)

nodes.title: Epidemic algorithms for replicated database maintenance
nodes.venue: ACM Symposium on Principles of Distributed Computing (PODC)
nodes.access_note: Free to read at ACM Digital Library (bronze OA). Not redistributed; link only.
nodes.abstract: When a database is replicated at many sites, maintaining mutual consistency among the sites in the face of updates is a significant problem. This paper describes several randomized algorithms for distributing updates and driving the replicas toward consistency. The algorithms are very simple and require few guarantees from the underlying communication system, yet they ensure that the effect of every update is eventually reflected in all replicas. The cost and performance of the algorithms are tuned by choosing appropriate distributions in the randomization step. The algorithms are closely analogous to epidemics, and the epidemiology literature aids in understanding their behavior. One of the algorithms has been implemented in the Clearinghouse servers of the Xerox Corporate Internet, solving long-standing problems of high traffic and database inconsistency.
nodes.key_problem: Keep the copies of a database replicated at many sites mutually consistent as updates arrive.
methods: Randomised algorithms for distributing updates between sites
Analysis by analogy with epidemics, using the epidemiology literature
findings: Every update is eventually reflected in all replicas while requiring few guarantees from the network
One algorithm was deployed in the Xerox Corporate Internet Clearinghouse servers
limitations: Concerned with spreading known updates - it does not infer any unobserved structure
Organiser read (repaired) abstract only

nodes.title: Network delay inference from additive metrics
nodes.access_note: Open access (arXiv math/0604367v2). Full text reviewed by organiser.
nodes.abstract: We use computational phylogenetic techniques to solve a central problem in inferential network monitoring. More precisely, we design a novel algorithm for multicast-based delay inference, that is, the problem of reconstructing delay characteristics of a network from end-to-end delay measurements on network paths. Our inference algorithm is based on additive metric techniques used in phylogenetics. It runs in polynomial time and requires a sample of size only poly(log n). We also show how to recover the topology of the routing tree.
nodes.key_problem: Multicast-based delay inference: reconstruct the delay characteristics of network links, and the routing tree topology, from end-to-end delay measurements.
methods: Additive (tree) metric techniques from phylogenetics
Use only 'short' paths to keep sample complexity low (building on Erdős et al.)
findings: Polynomial-time algorithm needing a sample of size only poly(log n)
Shows how to recover the topology of the routing tree
limitations: Primarily theoretical, with provable guarantees
Assumes multicast probing on a routing tree
evidence_refs: Full text arXiv:math/0604367 p.1 (abstract), p.5 (related work), p.7 (sample complexity)

nodes.title: Network Tomography: Estimating Source-Destination Traffic Intensities from Link Data
nodes.venue: Journal of the American Statistical Association
nodes.access_note: Paywalled (JASA). Abstract and bibliographic metadata only.
nodes.abstract: The problem of estimating the node-to-node traffic intensity from repeated measurements of traffic on the links of a network is formulated and discussed under Poisson assumptions and two types of traffic-routing regimens: deterministic (a fixed known path between each directed pair of nodes) and Markovian (a random path between each directed pair of nodes, determined according to a known Markov chain fixed for that pair). Maximum likelihood estimation and related approximations are discussed, and computational difficulties are pointed out. A detailed methodology is presented for estimates based on the method of moments. The estimates are derived algorithmically, taking advantage of the fact that the first and second moment equations give rise to a linear inverse problem with positivity restrictions that can be approached by an EM algorithm, resulting in a particularly simple solution to a hard problem. A small simulation study is carried out.
nodes.key_problem: Estimate node-to-node (source-destination) traffic intensities from repeated measurements of traffic on network links.
methods: Poisson traffic model with deterministic or Markovian routing
Method of moments leading to a linear inverse problem with positivity restrictions, solved by an EM algorithm
findings: A simple estimation procedure for a hard problem; small simulation study
limitations: Routing is assumed KNOWN (fixed paths or a known Markov chain) - topology is not inferred
Poisson assumption
Organiser read abstract only

nodes.title: ARACNE: An Algorithm for the Reconstruction of Gene Regulatory Networks in a Mammalian Cellular Context
nodes.access_note: Open access (BMC Bioinformatics). Full text reviewed by organiser.
nodes.abstract: BACKGROUND: Elucidating gene regulatory networks is crucial for understanding normal cell physiology and complex pathologic phenotypes. Existing computational methods for the genome-wide "reverse engineering" of such networks have been successful only for lower eukaryotes with simple genomes. Here we present ARACNE, a novel algorithm, using microarray expression profiles, specifically designed to scale up to the complexity of regulatory networks in mammalian cells, yet general enough to address a wider range of network deconvolution problems. This method uses an information theoretic approach to eliminate the majority of indirect interactions inferred by co-expression methods. RESULTS: We prove that ARACNE reconstructs the network exactly (asymptotically) if the effect of loops in the network topology is negligible, and we show that the algorithm works well in practice, even in the presence of numerous loops and complex topologies. We assess ARACNE's ability to reconstruct transcriptional regulatory networks using both a realistic synthetic dataset and a microarray dataset from human B cells. On synthetic datasets ARACNE achieves very low error rates and outperforms established methods, such as Relevance Networks and Bayesian Networks. Application to the deconvolution of genetic networks in human B cells demonstrates ARACNE's ability to infer validated transcriptional targets of the cMYC proto-oncogene. We also study the effects of misestimation of mutual information on network reconstruction, and show that algorithms based on mutual information ranking are more resilient to estimation errors. CONCLUSION: ARACNE shows promise in identifying direct transcriptional interactions in mammalian cellular networks, a problem that has challenged existing reverse engineering algorithms. This approach should enhance our ability to use microarray data to elucidate functional mechanisms that underlie cellular processes and to identify molecular targets of pharmacological compounds in mammalian cellular networks.
nodes.key_problem: Reverse-engineer gene regulatory networks in mammalian cells from microarray expression profiles.
methods: Pairwise mutual information between genes
Data Processing Inequality (DPI) to remove indirect interactions
findings: Exact (asymptotic) reconstruction when loops are negligible
Outperforms Relevance Networks and Bayesian Networks on synthetic data
Recovers validated cMYC targets in human B cells
limitations: All network nodes are observed genes - no hidden nodes are introduced
Sensitive to mutual-information estimation error
Networks with many loops are only approximately recovered
evidence_refs: Full text (BMC open access) p.5 (Theorems 1-3, relation to Chow-Liu)

nodes.title: A few logs suffice to build (almost) all trees (I)
nodes.access_note: Paywalled (Wiley). Abstract and bibliographic metadata only.
nodes.abstract: A phylogenetic tree, also called an “evolutionary tree,” is a leaf-labeled tree which represents the evolutionary history for a set of species, and the construction of such trees is a fundamental problem in biology. Here we address the issue of how many sequence sites are required in order to recover the tree with high probability when the sites evolve under standard Markov-style i.i.d. mutation models. We provide analytic upper and lower bounds for the required sequence length, by developing a new polynomial time algorithm. In particular, we show when the mutation probabilities are bounded the required sequence length can grow surprisingly slowly (a power of log n) in the number n of sequences, for almost all trees.
nodes.key_problem: How many sequence sites are needed to recover a phylogenetic tree with high probability under Markov mutation models?
methods: A new polynomial-time tree reconstruction algorithm
Analytic upper and lower bounds on required sequence length
findings: With bounded mutation probabilities the required sequence length grows only as a power of log n for almost all trees
limitations: Theoretical; assumes i.i.d. Markov-style site evolution
Organiser read abstract only
evidence_refs: Characterised in Choi et al. 2011 p.4 and Bhamidi et al. 2010 p.7

nodes.title: Network Tomography Based on Additive Metrics
nodes.access_note: Published version paywalled (IEEE); author preprint open on arXiv (0809.0158). Full text of the preprint reviewed by organiser. A conference version appeared at CISS 2008 (doi:10.1109/CISS.2008.4558692).
nodes.abstract: Inference of the network structure (e.g., routing topology) and dynamics (e.g., link performance) is an essential component in many network design and management tasks. In this paper we propose a new, general framework for analyzing and designing routing topology and link performance inference algorithms using ideas and tools from phylogenetic inference in evolutionary biology. The framework is applicable to a variety of measurement techniques. Based on the framework we introduce and develop several polynomial-time distance-based inference algorithms with provable performance. We provide sufficient conditions for the correctness of the algorithms. We show that the algorithms are consistent (return correct topology and link performance with an increasing sample size) and robust (can tolerate a certain level of measurement errors). In addition, we establish certain optimality properties of the algorithms (i.e., they achieve the optimal l-infinity-radius) and demonstrate their effectiveness via model simulation.
nodes.key_problem: Infer the routing topology and link performance from a source to a set of end hosts using end-to-end measurements.
methods: General framework built on additive metrics (path metric = sum of link metrics)
Neighbor-Joining (NJ) and a new Rooted Neighbor-Joining (RNJ) algorithm
Distance-based polynomial-time inference algorithms
findings: Algorithms are consistent and robust to bounded measurement error
RNJ achieves the optimal l-infinity radius
Effectiveness shown by model simulation
limitations: Assumes tree-shaped routing and an additive metric
Evaluation by model simulation (preprint)
evidence_refs: Full text arXiv:0809.0158 p.3 (related work), p.5 (analogy), p.13 (Alg. 1), p.15 (Alg. 2)

nodes.title: Maximum likelihood network topology identification from edge-based unicast measurements
nodes.venue: ACM SIGMETRICS International Conference on Measurement and Modeling of Computer Systems (SIGMETRICS)
nodes.access_note: Paywalled (ACM SIGMETRICS). Abstract and bibliographic metadata only.
nodes.abstract: Network tomography is a process for inferring "internal" link-level delay and loss performance information based on end-to-end (edge) network measurements. These methods require knowledge of the network topology; therefore a first crucial step in the tomography process is topology identification. This paper considers the problem of discovering network topology solely from host-based, unicast measurements, without internal network cooperation. First, we introduce a novel delay-based measurement scheme that does not require clock synchronization, making it more practical than other previous proposals. In contrast to methods that rely on network cooperation , our methodology has the potential to identify layer two elements (provided they are logical topology branching points and induce some measurable delay). Second, we propose a maximum penalized likelihood criterion for topology identification. This is a global optimality criterion, in contrast to other recent proposals for topology identification that employ suboptimal, pair-merging strategies. We develop a novel Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) procedure for rapid determination of the most likely topologies. The performance of our new probing scheme and identification algorithm is explored through simulation and Internet experiments.
nodes.key_problem: Discover network topology solely from host-based unicast measurements, without cooperation from internal routers.
methods: Delay-based unicast measurement scheme needing no clock synchronisation
Maximum penalised likelihood criterion for topology
Markov chain Monte Carlo search over topologies
findings: Can identify layer-2 branching points that induce measurable delay
Evaluated in simulation and Internet experiments
limitations: Global search is more expensive than pair-merging strategies
Organiser read abstract only

nodes.title: Network Tomography: Recent Developments
nodes.access_note: Open access at Project Euclid. Review article (secondary source). Abstract reviewed; automated full-text download was blocked by the host.
nodes.abstract: Today’s Internet is a massive, distributed network which continues to explode in size as e-commerce and related activities grow. The heterogeneous and largely unregulated structure of the Internet renders tasks such as dynamic routing, optimized service provision, service level verification and detection of anomalous/malicious behavior extremely challenging. The problem is compounded by the fact that one cannot rely on the cooperation of individual servers and routers to aid in the collection of network traffic measurements vital for these tasks. In many ways, network monitoring and inference problems bear a strong resemblance to other “inverse problems” in which key aspects of a system are not directly observable. Familiar signal processing or statistical problems such as tomographic image reconstruction and phylogenetic tree identification have interesting connections to those arising in networking. This article introduces network tomography, a new field which we believe will benefit greatly from the wealth of statistical theory and algorithms. It focuses especially on recent developments in the field including the application of pseudo-likelihood methods and tree estimation formulations.
nodes.key_problem: Survey network tomography: inferring internal network characteristics that are not directly observable.
methods: Review of pseudo-likelihood methods and tree-estimation formulations
findings: Network monitoring problems resemble other inverse problems; tomographic image reconstruction and phylogenetic tree identification have interesting connections to networking problems
limitations: Review article - a secondary source; claims should be traced to the primary papers it cites
Organiser read abstract only
